f-date.claim: The battle of Salamis was fought in 480 BC, traditionally dated to late September.
cites: Barry Strauss, The Battle of Salamis (2004)

f-laurium.claim: Years earlier Themistocles had persuaded Athens to spend a rich new silver strike from the Laurium mines on warships instead of sharing the money out.

f-athens-ships.claim: Athens supplied the largest contingent of the Greek fleet: 180 ships.

f-trap.claim: Modern historians read the message as a deliberate trap to force the battle into the narrow strait.
cites: Barry Strauss, The Battle of Salamis (2004)

f-artemisia.claim: Artemisia, queen of Halicarnassus, chased by an Athenian ship, rammed and sank a ship from her own side.

f-ram-weapon.claim: A trireme's main weapon was a bronze ram fixed at the waterline of its bow.
cites: J. S. Morrison, J. F. Coates and N. B. Rankov, The Athenian Trireme (2nd ed.) (2000)

f-rowers.claim: A trireme carried about 170 rowers on three levels and about 200 men in all.
cites: J. S. Morrison, J. F. Coates and N. B. Rankov, The Athenian Trireme (2nd ed.) (2000)

f-first-ram.claim: Herodotus says the Athenian Ameinias of Pallene was the first to ram an enemy ship; when the ships locked together, others came to help and the battle began.

f-aeschylus-ram.claim: Aeschylus says a Greek ship began the ramming and smashed off the curved stern of a Phoenician ship.

f-narrows.claim: In the narrow strait the crowded Persian ships could not use their numbers; they struck each other with their bronze rams and broke their oars.

f-fleet-size.claim: Aeschylus puts the Greek fleet at about 310 ships and Xerxes' fleet at 1,207.
cites: Barry Strauss, The Battle of Salamis (2004)

f-athlit.claim: The largest ancient warship ram ever found, the Athlit ram, was discovered off Israel in 1980: one piece of cast bronze, about 2.26 metres long and 465 kilograms. It comes from a later warship, not from Salamis.
cites: L. Casson and J. R. Steffy (eds.), The Athlit Ram (1991)
